source_document.body:
With the possibility of the New York City Delivery Protection Act headed toward some sort of amended structure and then a vote in the New York City Council before the end of the year, the push against it has ramped into high gear.
The opponents who have become increasingly visible just in the past few weeks–it’s tough to watch television in New York these days and after a little while not see one of their ads –have held onsite rallies and found an active media voice writing on the issue in a mostly critical way in The New York Post.
Its latest article cites Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) warnings that the Act, if passed as is, could add $5 to every package it delivers in the city.
That brought a retort on X from Council Speaker Julie Menin, whose views on how the final version of the Act will look are considered vital to its outcome,
It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections. We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs. If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6 — Speaker Julie Menin (@SpeakerMenin) November 19, 2026
The battle at times is taking on unusual political positioning. If it is assumed that the main target of the bill is Amazon–even though other companies like FedEx (NYSE: FDX) will be greatly affected as well–some of the arguments being made against the bill by the collection of direct service providers operating under the banner of the New York Delivers Coalition are muddying a traditional left/right dichotomy.
Amazon has long been a target of politicians on the left. Sen. Bernie Sanders has ripped the company’s “corporate greed.” Former vice president and Democratic Presidential candidate Kamala Harris suggested Amazon and other big tech companies should be regulated . And Democratic Socialist Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was seen as a key reason in her first term why Amazon pulled out of its plans to build an East Coast headquarters in New York City, having led the opposition to the plan (with Amazon eventually choosing northern Virginia as its site.)
That hasn’t changed in New York City, with Democratic Socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani actively backing the Delivery Protection Act.
Not normally heard from Amazon backers
In the last two weeks, New York Delivers has staged a demonstration on the steps of New York City Hall and were planning Thursday to protest at the district headquarters of Tiffany Caban, the member of the Council who introduced the Delivery Protection Act last year.
But this stepped-up opposition is coming with actions and statements that seem more out of a New York demonstration from the left than actions that implicitly could be seen as supporting Amazon, a corporation long vilified by the left.
For example, at the City Hall rally, one of the speakers commenced the chant of “No Justice, No Peace!” which has long been identified as the protest motto of The Rev. Al Sharpton.
And at the latest public media conference , ostensibly called to discuss the legal issues with the Delivery Protection Act seen by its opponents, the issue of race came up repeatedly and dominated the discussion far more than possible litigation. It echoed similar statements from the November 12 rally at City Hall.
“The Council should consider the burden that this legislation would place on business owners as well as their employees,” Derek Sells, chairman of the Cochran Law Firm that is the outside counsel to New York Delivers, told the gathering.
But he then raised a racial aspect of the bill.
Racial makeup at the DSPs
Sells cited research by AKRF, a consulting firm, that said “80% of last mile delivery workers are people of color, 88% live in New York City, and 49% live in state-designated disadvantaged communities,” Sells said.
The study estimates that between 3,000 and more than 10,000 workers could lose their jobs, according to Sells.
Mark Morial, the former mayor of New Orleans and now the CEO of the National Urban League, said at the media conference that “it was puzzling to me why a city that considers itself in the progressive mode would even see legislation like this as helping workers. In fact, it would destroy the businesses owned by the people standing with me, as well as many others, with no guarantee for their workers, with no compensation for their losses.”
That sort of discussion took up most of the roughly half-hour session with specifics on the legal issues few and far between.
Laying it out in a letter
But it was in a nine-page letter to Speaker Menin that the law-based arguments were explored in greater depth.
The core of the Delivery Protection Act is that one, delivery companies in New York City would need a license to operate; two, those companies can not hire subcontractors; three, the delivery companies would be required to hire any workers displaced by the end to subcontracting; and four, the licenses can be yanked for violation of any number of rules.
It is projected that if the bill is adopted with its original wording (though an overhaul of the language is expected), it would require Amazon to purchase its roughly 100 DSPs operating in the city because of the no subcontracting rule and turn their workers into employees of Amazon rather than their current DSP.
The Teamsters have strongly backed the Delivery Protection Act. The union has sought to unionize direct employees of Amazon, with a recent success in Canada and a long frustrating battle elsewhere in New York City.
To unionize the DSP drivers has been an even tougher challenge.
Sells’ letter cites three broad areas where he thinks the Delivery Protection Act is legally problematic.
First, “Federal law limits the ability of cities and states to dictate how delivery companies operate, including how they organize their delivery services and who performs the work,” Sells’ letter says.
Second, the law also conflicts with New York code, according to Sells. “New York State already has laws that determine when delivery drivers must be classified as employees and when companies can legally use independent businesses to perform delivery work. Intro 518 (another term for the Delivery Protection Act) would prohibit business arrangements that state law already allows and regulates,” Sells writes.
The third point, Sells said, is that the city can not override either federal or state law.
“Intro 518 also appears to reach drivers and businesses operating outside the five boroughs, including facilities in New Jersey, Westchester, and Long Island,” Sells’ letter says. “This raises additional legal questions about the City’s authority to regulate businesses beyond its borders and its impact on interstate commerce.”
The Sells letter also gets into some of the same issues heard from the steps of City Hall: the racial makeup of the DSP work force as well as the company owners, issues that may have political heft but are questionable as legal matters.
But where Sells ties them together is arguing that lawsuits that would follow the introduction of the Delivery Protection Act could drag on a long time, and it would be people of color most affected by that uncertainty.
The law, “if enacted, would invite years of costly litigation with a substantial risk that the Act’s core would be struck down, leaving workers without the protections the Council intends while the small businesses that employ them close in the interim,” the Sells letter said. “Those harms would fall most heavily on Black, Latino, immigrant, and outer-borough New Yorkers.”
F4A makes an appearance
One of the legal arguments raised by Sells is that the Delivery Protection Act could be in conflict with the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act (F4A).
That law has the well-known provision that states are barred from taking action that could impact a “price, route or service.”
It had been at the core of the now-settled legal dispute over California’s AB5 independent contractor law, and more recently was tossed out as a shield against broker liability in the case of Montgomery vs. Caribe Transport II.
Sells cited federal precedents that found laws Sells views as similar to the Delivery Protection Act regarding independent contractor status or hiring requirements were in violation of F4A.
Sells says the Delivery Protection Act “goes further” than the laws that were the subject of the earlier precedents cited in his letter.
Sells’ letter said he “anticipates” that the Act’s backers might turn to the safety exception of F4A to thwart the proposed law from overriding the act in its entirety. The safety exception allows state action like a tort in an action that might otherwise be seen as impacting a “price, route or service.”
“Anticipating” that the backers of the Act might counter with the safety exception–which applies to motor vehicles–as providing justification for the Act despite the rest of F4A, Sells says “a rule dictating the corporate identity of a driver’s employer, and banning an entire category of business relationship, regulates business structure, not vehicles.”
